571.s: Allen and Russell ask about the first tune played at Manny's, and about the old custom of playing a piece twice or more when dancers applauded. Lewis says it faded once dancing stopped.

571.t: Dance repertoire at Manny's: waltzes and old numbers
571.s: Lewis lists the old popular numbers and waltzes the band played for dancers, never speeding the waltz into foxtrot tempo. Bourbon Street bands no longer play waltzes.
571.q: Well, we had a repertoire that we played like, we played a lot of the old poplin numbers, like the girl that you married was one. We used to play rumbles. We played practically everything. During those days.

182.t: Dance repertoire in Delacroix: lancers, mazurkas, La Paloma
182.s: Tom describes what people in Delacroix danced to, mazurkas, waltzes and two steps, and the Spanish number La Paloma that Johnny Gould played.
182.ch: Playing in the country and Delacroix
182.q: We used to play sometimes, well we used to play, not Charters, call it Lancers, but we used to play Lancers at them times. You understand? But they don't play that no more. 182.s: Tom says Cajuns wanted waltzes and two steps, nobody sang in French, and a girl sang with the band in later years.
182.ch: Playing in the country and Delacroix
182.q: Well, Cajuns, anything. Waltz, some of them couldn't dance no mazookas. Most of them islands, Spanish people used to dance mazookas. 182.s: Bands played mostly blues, then quadrilles, lancers and varieties at dances.

254.t: Quadrille music, calling and how it was danced
254.s: Questions on quadrille music: the same band played special tunes, a caller directed the figures, and couples tried to outdance each other.
254.q: Do you speak? They have the band now. You see, the band of the only one tune. Oh, I see. You see, that band, any music that you want, that they know of. Yeah. Yeah.

254.s: Talk about popular tunes and dances of the period: waltzes, slow drag, the ping pong, turkey trot, bunny hug and grizzly bear.

254.q: Well, you know, she used to like it's beer, you see. Beer? And me, I never drink. Yeah. Yeah, you understand, you come up to it, you get beer. I guess they give it somewhere, you go on the beach, you see. And you see how it's going to come down and you all go out here. I don't know.

710.t: Dances Bailey knew: kick the bucket, slow drag, quadrilles
710.s: Bailey describes old dances, which ones he danced, and the quadrilles and waltzes watched for prizes.

710.t: Old dances: ball and jack, eagle rock, shake that thing, the bucket

Blow the breeze that's the olden time dance. Ain't the dance that has the game. Ain't the dance that has the game. This is uh the lindy hop. The…

710.s: Allen asks about Mardi Gras floor dancing; Bailey names the elephant dance and describes the puppy.
710.q: Well some of them get down on their knees they call that uh some of them used to name it the elephant dance. Elephant dance.

269.q: Oh, yes. When I'd go to the dances, you know. We didn't call it dance. They didn't call them dance. They called them ball.

601.s: Colored dancers did the waltz, schottische, two-step, slow drag and cakewalk, often for prizes until midnight. Martin says bands then played from midnight to four in the alley-type places.

601.s: Martin says dancers recognized a schottische, waltz or two-step at once, and bands did not sing except when asked for a song, then played it twice. Tom adds that the quadrille came on around eleven o'clock, followed by a mazurka.
601.q: Well now, the people played dance music... Yeah. In them days. If they played one of the dancers' sharders, they played a sharders. Well you don't dance a sharders. 292.t: Strict father, turkey trot, black bottom and Big Apple
292.s: As a teenager under a strict father she loved jazz mixed with ragtime; dances she did and the Golden Age club dances today.
292.q: Yeah, when I was a teenager, my father was very, very strict. He couldn't. But I loved jazz all the time. But I think there was a lot of ragtime mixed with the jazz. I don't think it was jazz. I think they mixed more ragtime with it.

292.t: Phonographs, waltzes and quadrilles before radio
292.s: She describes long-horn phonographs, waltzing, two-steps, polka and quadrille before radio.
292.q: I don't know, it was some kind of different step. Your mother would know if you'd ask, I bet you. She heard of it.

292.t: Mother's dances, Golden Age club and old records
292.s: Her mother's old dances, Golden Age club dancing, a carnival ball filmed by Walt Disney, and where old records can be bought.
292.q: Oh, she danced all those old-time two-steps and I used to hear her say the quadrille and the polka. The golden age, they have a lot of these two-steps and waltzes. 58.t: Stop time and tap dancers; cutting notes
58.s: Miller explains that stop time was made for tap dancers, that he played Sweet Suit behind them, and that cut notes do not fit a hot solo.
58.q: Well, I can try and answer that, I think. Maybe a guy would be getting off. But if he was getting off and cut his notes, he wouldn't do no good.

58.s: Punch recalls waltzes and two-steps danced for prizes and the freer dancing afterwards.
58.q: Well, it'd be righty dancing, but it wouldn't be for no prize. You know, after the prize was over, they did all kind of dancing. But there wasn't no such thing as jitterbug. Just two-step guys squatting on the floor and coming up, shaking, you know, and all like that.

58.t: Origins of stop time and George Boyd's piece Number One
58.s: Miller says stop time began with tap dancers and describes George Boyd's piece with band stops.
58.q: Well, I'd say, I wouldn't say Louis, I don't know, I swear, I don't know, just, they all started doing it, that's all I see. A fellow like, George Boyd, right, a piece they call number one, where he'd take a chord, the band stopped, and then the trumpet ticket, and the band stopped behind him, you…

65.t: Playing Afro-Cuban jazz and tipica without conflict

65.t: Why the mambo overtook Afro-Cuban jazz
65.s: Machito says mambo spread because American dance teachers made a dance for it, and anything danceable beat music to listen to.
65.ch: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
65.q: Because the American teachers or dance teachers, they learned or they create a dance for Americans to the mambo and the people --- any music that you could dance with is more popular than the one that you had to listen to. In those days, the big band era, yeah, it was fading, but still in the mind…

65.s: He names rumberos like Tanganito and Malanga as creative dancers, comparing them to Savoy dances in New York.

4.t: Playing classical toe-dance music at the Portola Louvre

4.ch: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
4.q: Oh, that was the big one. That was about it. It was popular like it was a... 'Course, right after that "Texas Tommy," then the "Ballin' The Jack" came out. "Ballin' the Jack" came out '16, "Texas Tommy" come out '10, '11 or '12. It was a fast dance, you know.

4.t: The Peckin' dance at the Follies Theater
4.s: Spikes first saw Peckin' about 1926 when Esvan Mosby's dance trio performed at the Follies, imitating chickens.
4.ch: Publishing, Jelly Roll in Los Angeles and band lore
4.q: Well, yeah, I think they did. The first time I seen it, "Peckin'"--you know, when I had the dance...when I had the band at the theater, he had a little trio--dance trio, and they come down there and did this "Peckin'" thing.

93.s: Green links the Pretty Foot to the cakewalk and demonstrates it and the polka-style Get on the Good Foot.

72.t: Rehearsals and tempo changes in Blake's band

72.t: Dances and dance tunes at the Victoria
72.s: Popular numbers included Stardust and Sweet Georgia Brown; people danced the Charleston, rhumba and Black Bottom.
72.q: The Charleston, yeah. A lot of time... We didn't have to actually play (?) time goes down. We did a lot of rhumbas.

869.t: Dances of the day, blues and the slow drag

827.t: Quadrilles, cakewalk revivals and French spoken at home
827.s: Arthur loves dancing; old-timers still perform quadrilles and cakewalks; his family spoke French at home.

1023.t: Did black bands see themselves as dance orchestras

1040.s: Which tunes went with each dance and tempo, and his waltz feature Peggy O'Neill.
1040.q: It was a two-step. They usually dance on Panama. Most of the dances that they danced, that was standard. A two-step and a slow drag, and a one-step. Now, the one-step, that was a tempo played about like when I played this number. Let's see what was that number I played.

1040.q: And that's what I was fixing to say. The waltz and the shardest, that was a popular dance. They contest you on the shardest. Oh, yeah? Yeah. You dance around right and left. You never stop turning. You go all the way to the other hall, and you keep turning. You never give up action. And the same…

620.t: Dancing the blues, slow drag, and whether blues are sad
620.s: He explains one-step, two-step and slow drag, playing a tune several ways, why blues are not necessarily sad, and that he cannot name blues singers.
620.q: Oh, yeah. You could dance that in one step or two step. Other than people, that's how they danced that, one or two step. They're playing them sometimes. And they had another dance they called a slow drag.

620.t: Ragtime, jazzing old tunes, waltzes and quadrilles
620.s: The early music was ragtime that people jazzed up; he played tunes as waltzes and charlotte pieces, never quadrilles, though he saw stage quadrille dancers.
620.q: See, they just jazzed most everything. Like them old-time charlots. I used to play a whole lot in charlots. There was a piece there they called Membrance. They called it Membrance. I remember they played that in the charlots. You could play in charlots, you could play in waltz. You mean they made a…

274.t: Ragtime and jazz arrive; no recordings; dance halls
274.s: Allen asks when jazz came, Labat says after World War I; none of them recorded; they recall dance halls.
274.q: You know, when the brass band would play for these places where they played for the dance, the brass band would take, like some of them numbers would take the chord of, you know what I mean, the trio, and they played for the dance. Some of them, the trio, some of them brass band, they were so…

274.t: Dances of the period and the band's supper table
274.s: Labat names dances such as the quadrille and black bottle, with a meal laid out for the band at intermission.
274.q: The quadrilla. They used to dance the quadrilla. And after the quadrilla. The men would take the quarter downstairs and eat gumbo or ham and salad. Oh, red beans. You see, when you come over here to play, man, they always had a table set for the band.

734.t: Dance repertoire: waltzes, mazurkas, card drill
734.s: The sets of waltzes, two-steps, schottisches, mazurkas and card drill, repeated over recesses at a dance.
734.q: Yeah, I played all, let me see, at that time he was playing a song that I played in my time. The first song I played on the clarinet was Next to Your Mother, Who Do Your Love. And I can't get the copy of that song. I never saw it either. Yeah. Da Next to your mother, Who Do Your Love. And well we…

734.t: Repertoire at the Villa: Dixieland, Charleston and blues
734.s: They played Dixieland, the Charleston craze, and blues in a modern way.
734.q: Oh no, no, we played real Dixieland. Dixieland style. Yeah, style, you know. And when I was there with Gabriel, the dance came out to call, what do you call that dance again? They go fast, you know, just faster you play the-

875.t: Five-minute dances and how sets were played
875.s: Howard explains how the five-minute dance worked, how the band used chord lists and music, and that the hall bands bought new stock numbers each week.
875.q: No, it depends. If you played a slow number, if you ain't play no more than two chords, fast or slow. Two chords. But when you play the five minute dance, that's the time you would get a chance of a piece of music you like, a song you like. Well then you'd play that all the way. By all the way that…

875.s: His first tunes came from Chris Kelly; description of jitney dance jobs with short choruses.
875.q: Well, my first tune, what I used to play, yes, that's my baby. And then I got saved about Chris. I played the blues by Maryland and Going Back to Jamaica. And mostly everything that Chris played that I knew that the folks was interested and liked it, I built up on that.

877.t: Music played for dinners, serenades and dances in Pass Christian
877.s: Handy describes sweet dinner music like Old Black Joe versus jazz for dances, in bands of six or seven including his father's.
877.ch: Early repertoire and the origins of jazz
877.q: Probably you would understand and probably you wouldn't and probably it would be just in my way of speaking. Or maybe it would be out of my way of speaking, but I'm going to see it this way. Which they would ask us before we'd come in to play dinner dance, dinner songs. Which is Old Black Joe and…

877.t: Dance styles: card trill and the shimmy
877.s: Handy describes old dances, the shimmy-she-wobble and fights over dancing with others' wives, while saying they always played jazz.
877.ch: Early repertoire and the origins of jazz
877.q: And they'd have the throwing out the halls and this one would dance with that one and then line this one would dance with that one. Because if they shake up to their lady they'd throw them out and cause a big fight and so on.

285.t: Opera House balls, waltzes and quadrilles
285.s: He did not play the French Opera balls; his band played waltzes, foxtrots and ragtime but not quadrilles.
285.q: Oh, yeah. They had about a 60-piece orchestra. Put that tablo on first, you know. And then they played nice sedate dances, waltzes, mazookas, foxtrotts and stuff like that, see.

285.t: One step, two step and the foxtrot
285.s: Lopez explains one step versus two step, tempo, and the later foxtrot, bunny hug and Texas Tommy.
285.q: Yeah, well, the one step, you make one step. And the two step, you made two steps.

837.t: Dance steps then and now: two-step, one-step, the Castles
837.s: He describes intricate close-contact two-step and one-step dancing, Irene Castle dancing to Piron's band at the St. Charles, and how dancing differs today.
837.q: Once, one or fewer, the younger people would. But the only dance that they had then at the time was the two-step, but that became extremely intricate. The steps had developed along with that. And it was not because the, what do you call them, the castles came. Irene Castle and Osborne came and…

837.t: Oliver at his peak and the slow march tempo of High Society
837.s: Oliver's playing polished up from the rough Big 25 days. High Society was originally a slow, dirge-like supper march, not a dance tune. Russell says Black dances used Gettysburg and the 6-8 in the same way.
837.q: That's one they clipped out for me on Golden Crest. And, well, even, I'm trying to think of some of the others that they used to sing. They were all foul. But anyway, many times, our group of six and seven-eighths wouldn't dance at all. Most of us would just hang around the band and watch and…

858.t: Old dances, the mambo and the shout
858.s: Dances then and now, waltzes and the shout, and Three Black Berries.
858.q: So, nowadays that they didn't do in the old days? Yeah. So, here's the Mambo, they didn't do that. Remember what old days? Yeah. The Mambo didn't do that in the old days. No. That's what I can think of right now. The only general, the old time, there was waltz. See, if a band couldn't play a waltz,…

858.t: Repertoire, waltzes and length of dance nights
858.s: Tunes the band played, how many waltzes per night, and the five or six hour dance sets.
858.q: Tisket or Tisket, and Heeby Jeeby, and the apple tree, and all such numbers like that in older times. Three o'clock in the morning, there's walls that we feature that. And sometimes, that's a number, no walls, sometimes. Yeah. They exactly teach you that too.

198.t: Playing a tune first as a waltz then in 4/4, as Thomas does
198.s: Asked about Thomas's habit of playing a tune as a waltz and then in 4/4, Barnes says it is not really right for every tune.
198.q: Well, I'll tell you how it is. It goes to rise if you want. Yeah. But we'd do it like when it's a lead band, I don't say we. A man would do it, would play that waltz. They'd clap it and they'd play a waltz back. Then if you like sitting down, you'll pick it up. Pick it up and give it to them, oh,…

198.t: Tunes played and bands competing on Sundays
198.s: He cannot recall the tune names, mentions Scott Joplin music, and describes bands showing off for club crowds on Sundays.
198.q: I don't believe I'm in Hummerwood or anything. I don't know Walla Holla. Go with me. I haven't forgotten that thing again. Sounds like down home right down. Mm-hmm. Wow, I can't think of that.

849.t: Waltzes and old numbers like My Blue Heaven
849.s: He praises waltzes and tells how Kid Howard started My Blue Heaven and how he relieved Howard when drunk.
849.q: They like waltzes. Planet White like waltzes. They like that. The color like that too. They like waltzes too. Well, I'll tell you the truth. You see waltzes? That's sweet music, man. That's sweet music, waltzes. Let me call you sweetheart.

849.t: Grand marches, call-outs and invitation-only society balls
849.s: Joseph explains how old bands opened balls with a march and call-out, and how invitations are now checked.
849.q: No, you started dancing. They started dancing. When you played the other way, they marched around the hall. You understand? When you played in a fox trough, well, that's where I'd grab and start dancing.

905.t: Frankie Duson and dances with quadrilles
905.s: Frankie Duson's trombone playing and the quadrille and shotis dances; also Joe Oliver and Buddy Petit.
905.q: What a little. You know, he didn't try to call him. That's Frank and Doocy. Yeah. That's what's up. That's a tramp all black. Yeah. Frank and Doocy. That was a slight tramp on you talking about. When you say good hair. That's all they used to call him.

905.t: Cajun audiences across the river; trumpeter Peter Armand
905.s: Dancers across the river, their taste in waltzes and blues, and a chauffeur-trumpeter named Armand.
905.q: I know the trumpet fly too. In New Jersey. My uncle will play electric guitar now. He used to play tenor banjos. Oh, I see. I'm not sure you'll see that old and old boy. I can tell you why you work there. Oh. You work at... Peter Armand.

203.s: Learning Tuxedo Junction, soloists, and how tempos suit dancers.
203.q: Well I can remember there was an arranger that brought tunes around after, when bands used to rehearse after, like two o’clock in the morning, you’d have a rehearsal after. He brought around an arrangement, which was “Tuxedo Junction.” And they worked on it you know, and I think that turned out to…

203.t: Opening and why the Swing Era was popular
203.s: Rowe introduces Best; they discuss why swing music was popular, with ballrooms and theaters full of dancers.
203.q: That’s a hard one. Well basically it was dance music, and of course the country was full of ballrooms in those days, and people liked to dance. Ballroom dance. And I think that was, between the ballrooms and the theaters, that was what they liked.

733.s: Music and dance go together in every culture; Person thinks jazz lost listeners by dropping dance.
733.ch: Influences: R&B, gospel and the church
733.q: No it’s together. Well every culture has dance, I mean regardless — even opera has ballet, you know, and country music has square dancing.

733.t: What swing is and the loss of dancing
733.s: Asked to define swing, Person says it is the element that makes the body move, and laments that jazz audiences now must sit still, with people leaving to go dance.
733.q: No. Swing — well to me swing contributes to an element in jazz that has been left out now. That’s why we have problems, is the element of dance and it makes the body move, and makes your feet move and makes you respond. That’s what swing is, I guess the little thing your body is — you go, if you…

146.t: Waltzes and sweet bands like Wayne King
146.s: Territory bands played stock waltzes for dances; Smith describes Wayne King and Guy Lombardo and how the band felt playing sweet repertory.
146.q: Yeah. They had most of the waltzes that they got from stocks. Because they were writing a lot of waltzes in those stocks during them days. Because Guy Lombardo and bands like those, and them hotel bands, they played a lot of waltzes. And we'd get some of them jobs where they couldn't make it, and…

146.t: Mutes, rumbas and hotel dance work
146.s: The band could not carry mutes for sweet music and played rumbas on hotel jobs; sweet bands ruled the North.
146.q: Uh-huh. Because they had different kinds of mutes in the trumpets and things, to get all that beautiful music. And them boys didn't have it. They wasn't buying them kind of mutes and things to get that pretty sound. They had two or three little mutes for Jazz or something like that. But all that…

231.t: Laying out the Buck and Bubbles act
231.s: The act opened with Rhythm for Sale, then gags, a dance, a piano solo, song medleys, a Spanish dance, request medleys and the main dance.
231.q: Then we'd go into a couple of gags. Then I'd go into a dance. Then go into a piana solo. Then from piano solo go into another song -- medley of songs like "Nobody Knows And Nobody Seems to Care," and then into a little Spanish dance where Buck dances with me and a Spanish duel. Then I go into piano…

231.t: The Dixon brothers, Doyle and Dixon, at the Palace
231.s: He recalls clog dancers Harlan and Darlan Dixon at the Palace in 1924-25, and Will Mahoney and Pat Rooney.
231.ch: Television, the stroke and later reflections
231.q: And Brothers. What about them? Harlan and Darlan is brothers. The Dickson brothers. What about them -- at the Palace Theater. Back in 1925, '24.

235.t: The post-war shift to listening audiences; enjoying dancers
235.s: After World War II people wanted to listen, which let Dizzy and Bird emerge, yet dance halls like Roseland endured; he enjoys seeing people dance.
235.q: : Well, the changes took place right after the war, you see, World War II. People wanted something different, so they were in a listening mood and that's how Dizzy and Bird and people like that were able to come to the fore. Because people were in a different mental frame of mind, they wanted to…

235.t: Playing for dancing versus playing for listening
235.s: Playing for dancers requires rapport and experience, and small-group players who came from big bands can balance dancing and listening.
235.q: Well, dance bands, playing for dancing is an experience that you have to feel. Now you playing a dance, 18-piece band, and you got two or three hundred people on the floor, you got

124.t: Waltzes and tangos at the Trianon Ballroom
124.s: Western dancers wanted waltzes, so the band played pop waltzes and authentic tangos with arrangements from Sampson and Dr. Steel.
124.ch: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
124.q: Trianon Ballroom -- that's the name of the ballroom. That's where all the big bands played when they came out there. That was the famous Trianon Ballroom.

124.t: Playing pop tunes and waltzes for the dancers
124.s: Songs had to be kept short; the band played all the popular music, show tunes and waltzes, which made the schools a good training ground.
124.ch: Dancing schools and Charlie Johnson in New York
124.q: tickets, you have a lot of dances. See, then we weren't supposed to play the songs but for so long, you know. "Hey, what are you doing? Cut that song off." We play a song like "Dinah." We'd play it a nice little length and end it, you know.

77.t: Songs and dances she says she introduced
77.s: She says she introduced "Some Day, Sweetheart" and "A Good Man Is Hard to Find" in Chicago, and "St. Louis Blues" and the Black Bottom in England.
77.q: In -- 'Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day,' at the -- oh, that was in Liverpool. I introduced that song, 'Little Man, You've Had a Busy Day.' And speaking about -- oh, I want to come to that next.

77.t: The Charleston, Plantation Club and Jungle Casino
77.s: Albertson recalls the origin of the Charleston dance and the Jungle Casino; Hunter thinks Florence Mills was at the Plantation and says she went to Europe in 1925.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: Uh-huh. See, I left, went to Europe in '25, I think, my first trip.

172.t: How Silver Leaf differed from Tuxedo; quadrilles and blues
172.s: Tuxedo had better arrangements and practice; Silver Leaf played straight music, quadrilles were gone, and blues were played.
172.q: And then we had different ideas you know. Better ideas. You know how to make different own arrangements like that and practicing. And we used to get to... Oh Graff one I believe we called it you know. And something come out like that where the other bands would be playing. But we would just have a…

173.t: Dance programs: waltz, polka, mazurka, schottische and quadrille sets
173.s: He doesn't recall specific pieces but describes the order of dances at balls, including the Virginia reel.
173.q: What kind? We used to play waltz first, then polka, then a mazooka, and then a shardish, and then a square dance. We had to be alliances. Yes. Then you'd come back, waltz, polka, mazooka, shardish, and a variety. That's two square dances. You understand? Yes. And then when the next square dance…

859.s: Old dance bands played ragtime, waltzes and reels as written; Gabriel argues older music was harder.
859.q: Ragtime or what? They played ragtime, they played the waltzes, they played the shallots, well the shallots died out. Yeah. But they played the waltzes, they played the reels as much. That was really good. All that kind of stuff.

402.t: Routine at the Fern: four-minute slow drags and repertoire
402.s: Sal explains the ticket slow-drag routine at the Fern, the piano players, and tunes such as Tin Roof, Panama and High Society.
402.ch: Riddick band and the Fern dances
402.q: Well, the fine. Well, four minutes slow drag is, you know, the routine was this. Every fourth piece, everybody get a rest. The piano would play. The piano play. I could probably never play there. I could probably name any member piano player. We played there. Almond Hook, Eddie Shields, Von Hecht,…

864.t: Quadrilles and who still has the music
864.s: Quadrilles were going out by the time he began; he never played them, and Peter Bocage might have sets.
864.ch: Style and old New Orleans customs
864.q: Not when I started. Well, yeah, they were playing, but I mean I wasn't. They were still dancing, quadrilles, shatters, and walls. But I never played quadrilles. During my time, coming along, the quadrilles was going out. And now and then somebody will hire a band and ask them, can they play a…

244.s: Sets of eighteen dances had to be timed by beats per minute so each began on schedule.
244.q: Yes. To a certain extent. Uh, he would, uh, tell you what tempos to play. Uh-huh. And, uh, we had, say, eighteen dances during that time. The dances was in sets. You played so many dances to a set. And then the next number, number two. And then, uh, maybe number three dance, we had a waltz to play…

567.t: Dance steps and his last funeral, for Picou
567.s: White describes the dancing at Millenberg and his last funeral, for Picou, with the Excelsior and Onward bands going to the cemetery.
567.ch: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
567.q: Yeah, Carolina. . . . Booms.... DING DING DING DING DING DING DING DING Booms.... That's where you could dance at a wall or you could dance at a shardies. But mostly, most of the people who always did dance were shardies or walls. That was the walls. And shardies, they used to take that for…

82.t: Why jazz records sold: danceability, and Art Hickman
82.s: Kirkeby thinks the dance tempo and the new beat drove sales. Before that Columbia made dance-school medleys with Prince's Band, and he pushed for real dance bands such as Art Hickman's.
82.ch: Columbia and the first jazz bands
82.q: Well, oh, yeah, I think musically, I think musically, too, the band hit. It was something new and something that had a terrific lift, a beat as we call it now, and it, there it was. Before that, we at Columbia were using Prince's Band, making these 12-inch records of medleys, of tunes, which were…

871.t: Quadrilles and waltzes: orchestras versus jazz bands
871.s: Jazz bands like Kelly's did not play quadrilles; only the orchestras did.
871.ch: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
871.q: No, no, no, no. They called them jazz band. They didn't play that? No, they didn't play that kind of stuff. Only the orchestras played that.

917.t: Quadrilles and dance repertoire; playing with Perez and Kid Punch
917.s: Keppard recalls card drills, mazurkas, lancers, and quadrilles at the halls and playing with Mal Perez and others.
917.q: that started up, I was a young man that time, you know, of course, I didn't mean to be 69 years old, won't mean to shave, I'll be glad, Mr. Russell. You don't look like that. Yeah, well, I'll be glad to see that, and experience life, and I know what it's all about, you know, of course, these days…

773.s: Description of the quadrille, why it was dropped, ball suppers, and the dances of her youth.
773.q: You know what they cut out... And look, they used to play long tunes. It wasn't like y'all now. And they cut out all them quadrilles. They had quadrilles and large ones. And getting ready to have that quadrille. That was fun. Because if a man knew how to dance, he showed himself then. And when…

956.t: Playing dances, pit and any trombone chair
956.s: Asked about dance work, Henry says he learned to play everything and any trombone part.
956.q: I play anything, dance, jobs, sit down in the pit, any place where they're playing. Because when I learned how to play, I learned how to play everything just to be played, wherever the man wants you to play. Second, third, fourth trombone, anything on the trombone.

258.t: Quadrille dances with John Tonkin's band in Alexandria
258.s: He recalls playing quadrille music at a dance near Natchitoches with John Tonkin's band, stayed seven years, and was drummer when Tonkin died.
258.q: Well, I'll tell you what happened uh, sometime uh, later than what I'm speaking of now. I was a drummer in John Tonkin Band in Alexander, Louisiana. And we used to go play at a place, I would say about three miles from Natchitoches, you call down on Cain River. And after intermission of the dance,…

1000.t: Stomping off tunes and waltzes; today's teenage crowds
1000.s: Leaders counted off tunes; waltzes were played plenty in the halls, while teenagers now want rock and roll and small combos with a singer.
1000.q: Played plenty waltzes. Yeah, played plenty waltzes. That's all they mostly used to play, pretty waltzes. And especially these halls down there. Well, in the coppery's in the economy hall, that used to take too. You had to play waltzes. But on the late watch, when it's getting late, around 12…

625.s: Trotter used to play rumbas, last at Charity Hospital, and describes breakaway and swing-out dances like the Big Apple.
625.q: Well, that breakaway they called it and different things like that. That swing out, you know, throw the gun out and swing out like that, you know.

251.t: Water Gardens dance halls and band styles
251.s: Many dance halls shared the name Water Gardens; talk of Charleston bands and how bands copy each other.
251.q: practically everywhere where there was a dance hall or some place like that used the word they used the same name all of a sudden it was the same name well there was no no uh there was no violation of any any laws different towns did you make any difference did lazy daddy have a band yeah yes lazy…

186.s: An interviewer recalls dancing the quadrille and waltz at the Hopes Hall and the talk drifts into discipline; the block ends in ASR repetition.
186.q: Waltz was a beautiful dance. Two steps and all these kind of things. But you don't find that now. You find them people that scrubbing the floor, breaking your back and your neck. They don't dance like that now. They ain't throwing you that way.

264.t: A stable six-piece band, repertoire and white dances
264.s: The band never changed personnel; they played blues and old numbers like Tiger Rag, mostly white dances at the hotel and Romeo Park ball games.
264.ch: Technique and the Covington band's sound
264.q: No, no. That's the whole bunch right there. Because we liked it one another and we liked what we was doing. We just had to start playing together and we liked it.

995.t: Playing Dumaine's numbers versus stock arrangements at clubs
995.s: Asked whether the Dumaine tunes were played in dance work, he says the big clubs wanted stock arrangements; the rest is garbled ASR.
995.q: Well, after we started playing, see like all these big clubs, the Sun Yacht Club, and all this country. They started playing nothing with stock. They wouldn't play them. They would normally like the rice. They played mostly stock. They had to build their dear

817.t: Ballads, waltzes and the old jazz repertoire on record
817.s: He loved jazz first but also ballads and waltzes, and recalls two-bit club tunes and records of the Halfway House and NORK.
817.q: Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. I always go back and remember the pretty tunes, you know. I always loved ballads and pretty waltzes as well as these jazz tunes, you see. I just get a lot of kick out of playing all of them. I love the jazz first, but I also like to play ballads and pretty waltzes. In those…

712.t: His other pieces: Chow Chow, Dixie Queen, Fans and Glances
712.s: Interviewer asks about Hoffman's compositions; she describes the delicate character of his pieces.
712.q: Well, Fans and Glances comes under a little bit, and that voluptuous come under a different, you'd have to be a pianist or something like that. It would never be used at a dance or among young people. But he had that kind of a delicate idea to his pieces, his music and things, besides the ring time.

765.t: How a dance set is structured
765.s: Sets, waltz every fourth set, hours, seasonal slumps and the list of tunes.
765.q: Yeah, we were starting, we were jamming. They had the waltzes in between. That's what we were doing on the other side. It was the same thing. You see, about every fourth set we hit a waltz. We can like a medley. If we have no requests, well, we just play medleys maybe, anything we feel like. We had…

275.t: Dances he created: Peace Time Hop, Jeep, Palsy Walk
275.s: He describes dances he invented after World War II and in Chicago.
275.q: Well, yes, shortly after the Second World War, well I created a dance called the Peace Time Hop. The reason I called it the Peace Time Hop, going from wartime to peace, I thought it would be very appropriate at that time to call it Peace Time Hop, which became very popular in the East Coast and in…

276.t: Spano's tonk: piano, chair drumming and the dancing women
276.s: Nash describes Spano's at Liberty and Perdido, the old songs played and the grizzly bear, snatch bite and eagle rock dances.
276.q: Spano's tunk was at Libra and Perdida. And a guy playing the piano in there. Another guy beating the drumsticks on the chair, on the hard chair. And the folks at the outside would hear the music. They'd bust in there. Sometime I had much as 15, 20 women in there. And start dancing. While the guys…

403.t: Tunes and dances in Bolden's time
403.s: Jones recalls Funky Butt, waltzes, mazurkas and quadrilles, knows nothing of slow drag, and cannot say whether Careless Love or Buckets Got a Hole in It were played.
403.q: Well, the waltzing, the mazookas, and all like that. That's what he played for dancing. In Miami City, you hear the rag music that they danced, only when they had a quadrill. Late at night you're getting about ready to break up there. Quadrill. The zookas, the waltzing, all them kind of things. I…

724.s: He played by ear and had to mix waltzes and jump numbers at dances.
724.q: Oh at that time you had to play at that time, you had to play everything, you know, waltzes, people was dancing waltzes and a lot and... five shots and two steps and all.

47.s: The owner made the band play waltzes to protect the ceiling when the Charleston craze hit; discussion of tempo.
47.q: recall any sign like that but the that came down to where the owner of it that Joseph Joseph wouldn't let us made us play waltzes because he was afraid the ceilings would go down the whole damn Charles

776.s: The boats played stock published arrangements, and patrons still prefer pretty straight dance music with good rhythm.
776.ch: Fate Marable, Armstrong and the early bands
776.q: Well, they liked the regular straight music, the pox files and waltzes. One one steps of course, and that's what they call him in the early days, and that's what they mostly do. Most of the band played. Just great music. And of course, some of the fancy steps came along, but some of the youngsters…

632.t: Discovering local white bands that played good jazz
632.s: Steinau was surprised to learn that bands from his high school dances played excellent jazz and says he was never a good dancer.
632.q: but you you know one of the things that really struck me and i remember saying the names when uh was it columbia that came out with that sir with that series on jazz with uh russ papalia and uh uh yeah some of the old new orleans white bands what really what really surprised me listening to them…

846.t: Older generation, dancing and the treatment of hired musicians
846.s: Elders saw only a beat to dance to, objected to loud bands, and hired musicians, white or Negro, were fed in the kitchen.
846.ch: Society bands and white New Orleans attitudes
846.q: I don't think they understood it at all. It had a very definite beat, and the dancing steps were quite simple in the earlier days, although I remember before we finished college that with the days of coming to Charleston and all that stuff, they became quite complex. But always, never the dancers,…

819.t: Tempo of rags and dance music, Joe Verges and Don't Leave Me Daddy
819.s: Old dance tempos were slower; the talk moves to businessman's tempo and the writer of Don't Leave Me Daddy.
